title: The Altar Rebuilt and the Foundation Laid
summary: In the seventh month the returned exiles gather in Jerusalem and, led by Jeshua the priest and Zerubbabel, rebuild the altar and resume the daily sacrifices and the Feast of Tabernacles, though they are afraid of the surrounding peoples. In the second year they begin work on the temple itself. When the foundation is laid the priests and Levites lead praise, the people shout for joy, and the older people who remember Solomon's temple weep aloud, so that no one can tell the joy from the weeping.
story: Chapter 2 listed the returnees and settled them in their towns. Now they gather in Jerusalem, and the first thing they build is not a wall or a house but an altar. For about fifty years there had been no regular sacrifice at the temple site in the way the law of Moses commanded. By restoring it before anything else, the community declares what it is: a people gathered around the worship of the LORD. The chapter moves from the altar (verses 1-6) to the preparations for building (verse 7) to the foundation and its celebration (verses 8-13). Its mixed ending, with shouts and tears together, sets the tone for the rest of Ezra, where joy in God's faithfulness lives alongside grief at how small the new beginning is. Opposition, which is only hinted at in verse 3, will break into the open in chapter 4.
historical:
The seventh month (Tishri, in September and October) of the first year after the return, probably 538 or 537 BC, was the season of Israel's great autumn feasts, so it was natural to gather then. The foundation work began in the second month (Iyyar, in April and May) of the second year, likely 537 or 536 BC. Jeshua son of Jozadak was the grandson of the last high priest before the exile, and Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel was of the royal line of David, so the two leaders together represent the restored priesthood and the surviving house of David.

The chapter's account raises a historical question. Ezra 5:16 says Sheshbazzar laid the foundation, and the prophets Haggai and Zechariah, speaking in 520 BC, describe the foundation as being laid in their own day (Haggai 2:18; Zechariah 4:9). Some scholars think the writer of Ezra 3 has drawn together work from different periods. Others suggest that Sheshbazzar and Zerubbabel worked together in the early years, with Sheshbazzar as the official in charge, and that the work of 520 BC was a fresh start on the same foundations after the stoppage recorded in chapter 4. The Hebrew verb for laying a foundation can also mean restoring or repairing, which makes both accounts possible.
cultural:
The Feast of Tabernacles (also called Booths or Sukkot) was a seven-day harvest festival in the seventh month when Israelites lived in temporary shelters to remember the wilderness years (Leviticus 23:33-43). Numbers 29 prescribes a different number of sacrifices for each day of the feast, which is what verse 4 means by the number prescribed for each day. The daily burnt offerings, morning and evening, were the steady heartbeat of Israel's worship (Exodus 29:38-42; Numbers 28:3-8). Restoring them meant that Israel was once again offering itself to God every day.

The preparations in verse 7 deliberately echo Solomon's building of the first temple. Solomon had paid the people of Tyre and Sidon in food and oil for cedar from Lebanon, floated down the coast (1 Kings 5:6-11; 2 Chronicles 2:16), and the returnees follow the same route to Joppa. The organization of Levites from twenty years old (1 Chronicles 23:24-27) and the music of the sons of Asaph as David had prescribed (1 Chronicles 16 and 25) also follow patterns the returnees took to be binding. This is a community consciously rebuilding on the old foundations, in more than one sense.
literary: The chapter has two movements, each ending in worship. The first (verses 1-6) centers on the altar and repeats the phrase as it is written, stressing obedience to the law of Moses. The second (verses 7-13) centers on the foundation and climaxes in a scene of sound: trumpets, cymbals, responsive singing, a great shout, and loud weeping. The song in verse 11, “For He is good; for His loving devotion to Israel endures forever”, is the refrain of Psalms 106, 107, 118, and 136 and was sung when the ark came to Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 16:34) and when Solomon's temple was dedicated (2 Chronicles 5:13; 7:3). By using it, the writer links this humble beginning to the great moments of Israel's worship. The last verse holds joy and grief in a single, deliberately unresolved image, heard from afar.

outline.t: The altar rebuilt in the seventh month
The Feast of Tabernacles and the regular offerings restored
Masons, carpenters, and cedar from Lebanon
The work begins under the Levites
Shouts of joy and the sound of weeping

doctrines.note: The returnees begin with the altar, the place where a holy God could be approached through sacrifice on his own terms. Worship according to what is written in the law comes before any building project, showing that access to God is the center of the community's life.
The chapter's praise is sung responsively and with thanksgiving, using words from Israel's psalms. Worship here is communal, rooted in what God has done, and able to hold both rejoicing and lament.
The song celebrates God's loving devotion (hesed), his steadfast covenant love to Israel. The foundation is laid not because the people are strong but because that love has outlasted their exile.

words.note: Hesed, often translated steadfast love, loyal love, or here loving devotion. It is the faithful love that keeps covenant commitments, even to the unfaithful. The song of verse 11 celebrates it as the reason for the restoration: Israel had broken faith, but God's hesed endures forever.

Yasad, to found or establish, used four times in the chapter. It can mean laying a building's first foundations, and it can also mean restoring or re-establishing a structure. That range helps explain why Ezra 3, Ezra 5:16, and Haggai 2:18 can each speak of the temple's foundation being laid at different times.

Teruah, a shout or blast, used of the war cry, the trumpet signal, and the loud cry of joy in worship. In verses 11-13 it is the people's great shout of praise, which mingles with the weeping of the old. The word is also used for the trumpet blast on the first day of the seventh month (Leviticus 23:24; Numbers 29:1), the very day this chapter's offerings began.

christ: The chapter holds together two things the New Testament also holds together: real joy at a new beginning and honest grief that the beginning is small. The old men weep because this temple is far less than Solomon's, and the prophet Haggai, speaking to the same people, promised that the glory of the latter house would be greater than the former (Haggai 2:9). Jews in Jesus' day saw that temple enlarged by Herod, but the New Testament finds the greater glory elsewhere, in Jesus himself, in whom God dwells among his people (John 1:14; 2:19-21). The altar rebuilt here also belongs to a system of daily sacrifices that Hebrews describes as a shadow, fulfilled when Christ offered himself once for all (Hebrews 10:11-14). These are connections of fulfillment, not hidden meanings in the text: the chapter shows a people longing for God's presence, and the New Testament names where that longing is met.
questions: The returnees rebuilt the altar before their houses or walls, even while they were afraid. What would it mean to put worship first in a season of fear or rebuilding?
Some wept because the new temple was less than the old, while others shouted for joy. How do you hold gratitude for small beginnings together with grief for what has been lost?
The people sang words their ancestors had sung for centuries. What do old, shared words of praise give a community that new words cannot?
